ellmercodex

Documentación en español: consulta la introducción en español o, después de instalar el paquete, vignette("ellmercodex-es", package = "ellmercodex").

ellmercodex lets you use your ChatGPT plan from R through an ellmer chat interface: the models in your plan work as one more ellmer provider, with no API key. That makes it easy to bring language models into your R analysis workflows.

The package is independent of OpenAI and does not require an API key or the Codex CLI. It uses OpenAI’s documented “Sign in with ChatGPT” flow for open-source, locally hosted apps and the public Responses API.

The structured-output and tool examples are inspired by the blog post about ellmercodex.

Installation

Install the released version from CRAN:

install.packages("ellmercodex")

Or the development version from GitHub with pak:

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("simxnherrera/ellmercodex")

If you are upgrading from 0.1.x, sign in again with codex_login(): the authentication flow changed and earlier credentials are not kept.

Quick start

Check the local integration, sign in, and create a chat:

library(ellmercodex)

codex_available()
auth <- codex_login()

chat <- chat_codex(model = "gpt-6-luna", effort = "low")
chat$chat("Hello from R")
#> Hello! What are you working on in R?

codex_login() opens a browser window where you sign in with your ChatGPT account. Because chat_codex() returns an ellmer Chat object, most of the usual ellmer interface works: each $chat() call keeps the conversation history, and $stream() streams the response:

chat$stream("Give me three ideas for naming an R package.")

Once you have signed in, later sessions can call chat_codex() directly. With model = NULL, the package picks a usable model from your account’s catalog.

More than a chatbot

Because you are working with an ellmer Chat, you can ask for structured results instead of free text. For example, you can classify an excerpt from a Uruguayan parliamentary debate on cannabis regulation:

# A real excerpt from a parliamentary debate on cannabis regulation
excerpt <- paste(
  "seguimos pensando que además de la represión y del combate al",
  "narcotráfico que debe seguir con firmeza y decisión como sociedad",
  "debemos apostar a dos o tres pilares fundamentales la educación",
  "la prevención y la rehabilitación"
)

result <- chat$chat_structured(
  paste(
    "Classify the excerpt as PREVENTIVE, PUNITIVE, MIXED, or NO_CLEAR_STANCE.",
    "Use MIXED when it argues for preventive and punitive responses at the",
    "same time. Answer in English.",
    "\n\nExcerpt:",
    excerpt
  ),
  type = ellmer::type_object(
    stance = ellmer::type_enum(c(
      "PREVENTIVE",
      "PUNITIVE",
      "MIXED",
      "NO_CLEAR_STANCE"
    )),
    rationale = ellmer::type_string()
  )
)

result
#> $stance
#> [1] "MIXED"
#>
#> $rationale
#> [1] "The excerpt supports firm repression and combating drug trafficking,
#> alongside education, prevention, and rehabilitation."

For text analysis, this gives you a structure that R can put into a data.frame, validate, or analyze.

An agent inside R

You can also register R functions as tools that the model may decide to call during a conversation. Suppose you have already classified some speeches:

speeches <- data.frame(
  party = c("FA", "FA", "PN", "PN", "PN"),
  stance = c("PREVENTIVE", "MIXED", "PUNITIVE", "PUNITIVE", "MIXED")
)

Write an R function that summarizes one party’s stances and expose it to the model as an ellmer tool:

summarize_party <- function(party_name) {
  speeches |>
    dplyr::filter(party == party_name) |>
    dplyr::count(stance) |>
    jsonlite::toJSON()
}

summary_tool <- ellmer::tool(
  summarize_party,
  name = "summarize_party",
  description = "Count the policy stances in a party's speeches.",
  arguments = list(party_name = ellmer::type_string())
)

chat$register_tool(summary_tool)

chat$chat("Compare the policy stances of FA and PN. Use the available tool.")
#> FA has one **MIXED** stance and one **PREVENTIVE** stance. PN has one
#> **MIXED** stance and two **PUNITIVE** stances. Both have a mixed stance,
#> while FA's other stance is preventive and PN's are punitive.

The model can call summarize_party() for each party, receive the results computed by R, and use them in its answer. A tool could just as well query a database, search a corpus, run a calculation, or call an API.

R still runs the functions: the model can only use the tools you register explicitly, and it decides when to call them and with which arguments. Structured requests do not use registered tools, as in ellmer; gather tool-assisted context with $chat() first, then extract the result with $chat_structured().

Choose a model

Model availability depends on your account and workspace. Query the catalog after signing in:

models <- codex_models()
models[c("id", "display_name", "default_reasoning_effort",
         "supported_reasoning_efforts")]

The catalog does not always include every model the service accepts. You can pass a model ID explicitly even when it is absent from codex_models(), and the service validates the model and reasoning effort. For example, gpt-6-luna works although the catalog does not list it.

Reasoning effort can be supplied directly or through ellmer parameters:

chat <- chat_codex(model = "gpt-6-luna", effort = "max")

chat <- chat_codex(
  model = "gpt-6-luna",
  params = ellmer::params(reasoning_effort = "max")
)

Set ELLMERCODEX_MODEL to use a model without passing model each time:

Sys.setenv(ELLMERCODEX_MODEL = "gpt-6-luna")
chat <- chat_codex()

Async chat, cancellation, and files

The returned chat also supports ellmer’s asynchronous methods:

chat$chat_async("Summarize the conversation.")

controller <- ellmer::stream_controller()
stream <- chat$stream_async(
  "Write a short story.",
  stream = "content",
  controller = controller
)
# Pass `stream` to an async consumer such as a Shiny chat component.
# Call `controller$cancel()` from the UI to stop generation.

Images and PDFs work with ellmer’s usual content helpers:

chat$chat(
  ellmer::content_image_file("plot.png"),
  ellmer::content_pdf_file("report.pdf"),
  "Explain these files."
)

Authentication

codex_login() opens the browser so you can choose your ChatGPT account and workspace and allow ChatGPT plan usage. The first sign-in creates a registration bound to that account; later sign-ins reuse it. The credential is stored in tools::R_user_dir("ellmercodex", "config") (or ELLMERCODEX_HOME) with owner-only permissions.

Inspect sign-in state with a redacted account summary:

codex_account()

For a session that lasts only as long as the R process:

auth <- codex_login(persist = FALSE)

codex_logout() signs out, revokes the token, and removes the credential stored by this package. To switch accounts or workspaces, sign out and call codex_login() again.

Limitations

ChatGPT plan usage through “Sign in with ChatGPT” is an OpenAI preview: it needs an eligible plan and workspace, and its limits and features may change. During the preview, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and other arguments OpenAI excludes are not accepted; the package rejects them before sending a request.

The supported scope is interactive, single-conversation use of the public ellmer Chat object (ellmer 0.5.0 or later). Provider token counting, file management, and the separate parallel_chat*() and batch_chat*() helpers are not supported.

ellmercodex is an independent integration and is not affiliated with or endorsed by OpenAI.
